passages.t: The fading crown of Samaria's drunkards
passages.happening:
‘Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, the pride of those overcome by wine’ (verse 1).

The Lord has someone strong and mighty, like a hailstorm or a flood, who will smash that crown to the ground (verse 2). It will be trampled (verse 3). The fading flower will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest, which whoever sees it picks and swallows (verse 4).

‘On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people’ (verse 5), a spirit of justice to the judge and strength to those who turn back the attack at the gate (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
After the wide vision of chapters 24 to 27, the book returns to the streets of Samaria and Jerusalem. Chapter 28 opens a section, chapters 28 to 33, marked by a series of woes about the Assyrian threat and Judah's temptation to seek safety in alliances, especially with Egypt.

Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, stood on a hill rising above a fertile valley, like a wreath on a drinker's head. Isaiah's picture of a fading wreath on a drunk's head describes Samaria's leaders at the end of the party. The oracle must come from before 722 BC, when Samaria fell to Assyria after a siege of about three years. The strong and mighty one of verse 2 is Assyria.

An early fig, ripe before the main harvest, was eaten the moment it was found. Samaria would be swallowed as quickly. But when the false crown is gone, the LORD himself will be the crown of his remnant.
passages.later: Kings records the end: ‘the king of Assyria invaded the whole land, marched up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years’ (2 Kings 17:5).
passages.asks: Samaria's pride was a wreath fading on a drunkard's head. Ask what you are crowned with that is already fading. And ask what it would mean for the LORD himself to be your crown.

passages.t: Priests and prophets who reel, and line on line
passages.happening:
Jerusalem's leaders are no better. ‘Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine’ (verse 7). They stumble in their visions and their judgments. Their tables are covered with vomit (verse 8).

They mock Isaiah. Who does he think he is teaching, babies just weaned (verse 9)? To them his message sounds like ‘Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there’ (verse 10).

So God will speak to them through mocking lips and foreign tongues (verse 11), the people to whom he once said, ‘This is the place of rest, let the weary rest’ (verse 12). But they would not listen. So the word of the LORD to them will become that same babble, so that they stumble backward and are captured (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The religious leaders, the very people who should have taught God's word, are drunk at their own feasts. They mock Isaiah's plain teaching as if it were for toddlers.

The Hebrew of verse 10 is a string of short syllables, tsav latsav, qav laqav, which may imitate baby talk, a child chanting letters as he learns them, or the sound of a foreign language. The leaders' mockery is turned back on them. Because they would not listen to God's plain word, they will hear his word in the foreign speech of Assyrian soldiers.

God had offered rest: this is the place of rest, let the weary rest. They refused it.
passages.later: Paul quotes verses 11 and 12 as he writes about speaking in tongues: ‘By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me’ (1 Corinthians 14:21).
passages.asks: God offered his people rest, and they would not listen. Ask what rest God has offered you that you keep refusing. And ask whether you have ever mocked a plain truth because it seemed too simple.

passages.t: A covenant with death, and a stone laid in Zion
passages.happening:
‘Therefore hear the word of the LORD, O scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem’ (verse 14). They have said they made ‘a covenant with death’ and an agreement with Sheol, so that the coming scourge will not touch them, ‘because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place’ (verse 15).

So the Lord GOD says, ‘See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken’ (verse 16). He will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level. Hail will sweep away their refuge of lies (verse 17). Their covenant with death will be canceled (verse 18), and the scourge will carry them away morning after morning (verse 19). ‘Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you’ (verse 20).

The LORD will rise as at Mount Perazim and the Valley of Gibeon, ‘to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task’ (verse 21). Do not mock, or the chains will grow heavier (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The covenant with death is most often understood as a political alliance, probably Judah's dealings with Egypt in Hezekiah's reign. After Sargon II died in 705 BC, Hezekiah joined other states in revolt against Assyria and looked to Egypt for help, which led to Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC. Isaiah calls it a covenant with death, perhaps with a bitter play on Mot, the Canaanite god of death, or on Egypt's concern with the afterlife; some also see a reference to consulting the dead.

Against their refuge of lies, God sets his own foundation: a tested stone in Zion. The one who trusts it will not be shaken, or, as the Greek translation has it, will not be put to shame.

The bed too short and the blanket too small is a proverb for a plan that cannot give rest. Mount Perazim and Gibeon recall places where God fought for Israel, against the Philistines under David. Now his strange work is to fight against his own people.
passages.later: Peter and Paul both quote verse 16 of Christ: ‘See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame’ (1 Peter 2:6; compare Romans 9:33 and Romans 10:11). David once said at Baal-perazim, ‘Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me’ (2 Samuel 5:20).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that judgment is God's strange work and disturbing task?

Verse 21 recalls places where God fought for Israel against her enemies, then says he will now rise up in the same way against Jerusalem. The work is strange because it seems contrary to his character and his covenant: the God who defended Zion now brings enemies against it. Readers take this in two main ways. Some stress that judgment is truly foreign to God's heart, which delights in mercy: ‘For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death’ (Ezekiel 18:32). Others stress the shock to Judah: the leaders assumed God was on their side no matter what, and the strange work is his refusal to protect their sin.

Both fit the chapter. The farmer's parable that follows adds a third: God's judgment is not random or unlimited. The threshing does not go on forever, and its aim is to bring out the grain, not to destroy it.
passages.asks: The leaders made lies their refuge, and their bed was too short and their blanket too small. Ask what you have made your hiding place that cannot cover you. And ask what it would mean to build on the stone God has laid.

passages.happening:
‘Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say’ (verse 23). Does the plowman plow every day without end (verse 24)? When the ground is level, he sows caraway and cumin, plants wheat in rows and barley in plots (verse 25). ‘For his God instructs and teaches him properly’ (verse 26).

Caraway is not threshed with a sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin; they are beaten out with a stick and a rod (verse 27). ‘Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed’ (verse 28). The cart wheels roll over it, but the horses do not crush it.

‘This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with a parable from the farm. A good farmer does not plow forever. He plows, then sows. He treats each crop as it needs: delicate seeds like caraway and cumin are beaten out by hand with a stick, while grain is threshed with heavy sledges. And even grain is not threshed endlessly, or it would be crushed.

The farmer learned this wisdom from God. So God's own dealings are just as measured. His judgment has a time and a purpose, and it stops before it destroys.

The last line calls God wonderful in counsel, an echo of the royal name in 9:6, Wonderful Counselor. The first hearers, facing the Assyrian scourge, were given a reason to trust that it would not go on forever.
passages.later: Lamentations makes the same confession: ‘For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men’ (Lamentations 3:33). And Isaiah names the coming king ‘Wonderful Counselor’ (Isaiah 9:6).
passages.asks: The farmer does not thresh forever, because his aim is bread, not ruin. Ask whether you believe that about the hard season you are in. And ask what God might be bringing out of you through it.
